messages.subject: Question about mahalanobis distance matching
messages.body_plain:
Dear All,

I am trying to replicate the results from Dr. King's paper: Why PS should
not be used for Matching. Somehow I do not think Matchit with  mahalanobis
distance is giving me what I want

Below is the code:


n<-100

x1_contr<-runif(n,0,5)
x2_contr<-runif(n,0,5)

x_contr<-cbind(x1=x1_contr,x2=x2_contr)

x1_treat<-runif(n,1,6)
x2_treat<-runif(n,1,6)

x_treat<-cbind(x1=x1_treat,x2=x2_treat)

T<-c(rep(0,n),rep(1,n))

X.all<-rbind(x_contr,x_treat)


my.data<-data.frame(T,X.all)

rownames(my.data)<-paste("ID",1:dim(my.data)[1])

mdm.out<-matchit(T~x1+x2,data=my.data,distance=mahalanobis,mahvars
=c("x1","x2"), caliper=0.05,replace=FALSE)

summary(mdm.out)

Sample sizes:
          Control Treated
All           100     100
Matched       100     100
Unmatched       0       0
Discarded       0       0


How can all cases and controls be matched?

Thanks,

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Dear Swapnil,
You may find the tutorial I referenced in a post earlier this morning useful.    It will answer many of these sorts of questions.

But to answer them briefly:

1.  If the ratio of treated:control is about 1:1 to start with then a simple nearest neighbor matching without replacement (the default in MatchIt) won’t make a lot of sense. You may want to try exact matching (like CEM), matching with replacement, or full matching.

2.  Yes, you can use categorical covariates as predictors in the propensity score model.

3.  It is hard to say in advance what method will work best; see #1 above.

4.  Balance diagnostics can be used to study the quality of the approach; see the JSS paper link I sent around earlier.

Thanks,
Liz

messages.subject_clean: Controlling for preexposure PS model covariates in final models for outcomes?
messages.body_plain:
Hi All,

I have a question regarding the final statistical analyses used to compare
outcomes for matched cases and controls. I've noticed that several of you
who have worked to develop and support MatchIt introduce the pre-exposure
covariates used for the estimation of the propensity scores into the final
models used to compare outcomes. I hadn't seen this done prior to reading
several of your papers.

If matching has indeed successfully eliminated all observable differences
between cases and controls (ignorability) and all confounding and bias has
truly been taken into account -- how would you explain the rationale for
doing this? Would the "residual confounding" that this is supposed to
address be the extent to which the propensity score pre-exposure covariates
predict the outcome above and beyond their relationship with the treatment
condition?

I'll appreciate any thoughts you may have on this. Thank you in advance for
your help.

Best wishes,
Sharon

I found that the Mayo Clinic SAS macro worked well for me for optimal
matching with a large sample.

Sharon

Liz

Hi Susan,
This output, from match.data simply lists the units that were matched, not necessarily which was matched to which.

If you want pairs to always have one person with Interv=1 and Center=50 and the other person to have Interv=0 and Center=40 you should just code your “treatment” variable in that way, to be a 1 for people with Interv=1 and Center=50 and 0 for people with Interv=0 and Center=40.

See the other thread on the matchit listserv yesterday for more information on how to see who was actually matched to who; that information is in the match.matrix object.

Liz
